metadata.note: California's first railroad and the branch it grew into. The Sacramento Valley Railroad was incorporated on August 4 1852 and opened from Sacramento to Folsom on February 22 1856, 22.9 miles of 5 ft gauge laid along R Street and what is now Folsom Boulevard under Theodore Judah - the survey work that made his name before the Central Pacific. It was meant to reach the Comstock, and the Placerville and Sacramento Valley Railroad (incorporated June 12 1862) carried the rails on from Folsom to Latrobe in 1864 and Shingle Springs in 1865, where they stopped for 23 years while stages did the rest. Central Pacific bought control of the Sacramento Valley in August 1865, the two companies merged into the Sacramento and Placerville Railroad in 1877, and Southern Pacific took the whole thing in 1888, the same year the last miles into Placerville were finished. The features are split at each change of control rather than recoloured, per CLAUDE.md Rule 4, so the same corridor appears under four owners' colours as the years advance, plus the present-day heritage operation. Note that two different companies share the Placerville and Sacramento Valley name - the 1862 railroad and the 2008 non-profit that runs excursions on the same rails - and they are treated as the separate companies they are, with the incorporation year in the company string to keep them apart. GEOMETRY METHODOLOGY: traced from OpenStreetMap (Overpass) over all railway ways in the corridor, with the operator and line-name tags used as routing weights rather than filters, then a corridor-weighted Dijkstra between anchors and Douglas-Peucker simplification at 12 m. Every feature carries its own geometry_quality naming its approximated legs.

metadata.not_yet_sourced: The exact year passenger service ended. Two sources say only 'the early 1940s', and no timetable was consulted; the 1941 end year on the Southern Pacific segment is a placeholder for that phrase, not a sourced date. This also conflicts with the heritage operator's statement that its 2011 trains reached Latrobe 'for the first time in more than 50 years', which would put the last passenger train to Latrobe nearer 1960 than 1941 - the conflict is recorded rather than resolved. Also unsourced: all headways and average speeds; the intermediate station list and mileposts between Sacramento and Folsom (branchline.uk publishes no California volume, so the milepost check available for other layers could not be run here); and whether any passenger service ran over the Folsom - Latrobe section between the early 1940s and 2011.
geometry_sources: OpenStreetMap via Overpass API: all railway ways in a Sacramento - Placerville bounding box, chained by shared node ids and routed with a corridor-weighted Dijkstra that weights (rather than filters on) the name and old_railway_operator tags. Named ways used: 'Placerville Industrial Lead' (the surviving ex-SP freight track), 'SacRT Gold' / 'SacRT Gold East' (light rail laid in the same right of way), 'Placerville Branch', 'El Dorado Trail'.
The 1.65 mi from the Sacramento River levee east along R Street is hand-placed, not traced: OpenStreetMap maps only a 100 m fragment of that alignment.

https://celebratecalifornia.library.ca.gov/february-22-1856-maiden-run-of-californias-first-railroad-2/ and https://www.railswest.com/history/californiabeginnings.html (Judah's alignment ran along R Street and today's Folsom Boulevard; passenger terminal at 3rd and R, freight depot and turntable at 3rd and Front)

properties.speed_source: estimated for a 5 ft gauge line of the 1850s; not sourced from a timetable
properties.geometry_quality: Traced Sacramento - Folsom, 37 points, 22.4 mi against a documented 22.9 mi (-2.1%). The eastern 20.8 mi of the Sacramento - Folsom leg is real-traced from OpenStreetMap along the surviving right of way: 12.6 mi on the ex-SP freight track OSM names 'Placerville Industrial Lead' and 8.0 mi on the SacRT Gold Line light rail, which was laid in the same right of way and runs within a few tens of metres of it. APPROXIMATED LEG: the westernmost 1.65 mi, from the foot of R Street at the Sacramento River levee through the passenger terminal at 3rd and R and east along R Street to about 20th, is a 3-point straight line placed by hand. That alignment is documented - Theodore Judah laid the line along R Street and what is now Folsom Boulevard, and R Street runs dead straight - but OpenStreetMap maps only a 100 m fragment of it, so no trace was possible. Traced Sacramento - Folsom is 22.4 mi against a documented 22.9. ERA CAVEAT: the line is drawn on the corridor as it survives today. The Sacramento end in particular is the R Street alignment as documented rather than as surveyed, and no attempt was made to reproduce the 1850s track centreline within the corridor.

segments.note: The Sacramento Valley Railroad was incorporated on August 4 1852, the first railroad company incorporated in California. Construction began at Sacramento in February 1855 and the line opened to Folsom on February 22 1856 - California's first railroad, 22.9 miles, built to 5 ft gauge with Theodore Judah as chief engineer. The passenger terminal stood at 3rd and R Streets, with the freight depot and turntable at 3rd and Front. Central Pacific took a controlling interest in August 1865 and converted the line to standard gauge. Headway is an unsourced estimate; no timetable was consulted.

properties.line: Placerville and Sacramento Valley: Folsom – Shingle Springs
properties.speed_source: estimated; not sourced from a timetable
properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap, 149 points, 26.5 mi against a documented 26 mi (+1.8%). 25.9 mi of the routed path lies on ways OSM names 'Placerville Branch'; 38 m of straight-line bridging in total, longest 21 m. No approximated legs. The route is drawn on the surviving right of way, which runs Folsom - White Rock - Latrobe and then north to Shingle Springs.

segments.note: The Placerville and Sacramento Valley Railroad was incorporated on June 12 1862 to carry the Sacramento Valley's rails on toward the Comstock and the mines; construction east from Folsom began in late 1863 and the line reached Latrobe in August 1864. The full Folsom - Shingle Springs route is drawn from the outset, but only the Folsom - Latrobe portion was open in these years; Latrobe - Shingle Springs did not open until June 1865. Headway is an unsourced estimate; no timetable was consulted.

segments.note: The line reached Shingle Springs in June 1865, adding 26 miles to the route and making Shingle Springs the railhead for stage traffic to Placerville and the Nevada mines. The company kept its own corporate identity until it was merged into the Sacramento and Placerville Railroad on April 19 1877. Headway is an unsourced estimate; no timetable was consulted.

segments.note: Central Pacific acquired a controlling interest in the Sacramento Valley Railroad in August 1865 - buying out a line that had been its rival for the eastward route - and converted it from 5 ft to standard gauge. The Sacramento Valley kept its corporate name until April 19 1877, but the trains were Central Pacific's from 1865, which is why this feature carries Central Pacific's colour. Headway is an unsourced estimate; no timetable was consulted.

segments.note: The Sacramento Valley and the Placerville and Sacramento Valley were merged on April 19 1877 to form the Sacramento and Placerville Railroad, 49.1 miles from Sacramento to Shingle Springs, still under Central Pacific control - hence Central Pacific's colour for these years. Shingle Springs remained the end of track until 1888. Headway is an unsourced estimate; no timetable was consulted.

properties.geometry_quality: The full Sacramento - Folsom - Latrobe - Shingle Springs - Diamond Springs - Placerville route, 290 points, 61.1 mi against a documented figure of about 60 mi (+1.8%). The Shingle Springs - Placerville leg beyond the earlier terminus is 12.2 mi traced, 7.8 mi of it on ways OSM names 'Placerville Branch' and 3.5 mi on the 'El Dorado Trail' rail-trail that occupies the grade; a rail-trail wanders from the exact centreline, which is the likeliest reason this leg runs long. APPROXIMATED LEGS: the 1.65 mi hand-placed R Street leg at the Sacramento end (see svrr-sacramento-folsom), and a 1.29 mi straight line on the final approach into Placerville, from 38.7286,-120.8113 to the depot site, where the grade is not mapped. Everything else follows mapped track or mapped abandoned grade.

segments.note: The last 11 miles from Shingle Springs into Placerville were finished on March 29 1888, and on May 15 1888 the railroad passed to Southern Pacific through its Northern Railway subsidiary, becoming the SP's Placerville Branch. Southern Pacific took direct control on April 14 1898. Headway is an unsourced estimate; no timetable was consulted.

segments.note: Under direct Southern Pacific ownership the branch carried what its historians call a thriving passenger service to and from Sacramento until the early 1940s, serving combined freight-and-passenger depots at Latrobe, Shingle Springs, El Dorado, Diamond Springs and Placerville. The 1941 end year is a placeholder for 'the early 1940s' - no source consulted gives the exact year, and one later account implies passenger trains reached Latrobe into the 1950s (see the layer's not_yet_sourced field). Freight outlasted passengers by decades: SP stopped regular operation east of Folsom in 1986, ended Folsom - Placerville operations in August 1989 and sold the line to a public joint powers authority in 1996. Headway is an unsourced estimate; no timetable was consulted.

segments.note: A new Placerville and Sacramento Valley Railroad was incorporated on August 8 2008 as a non-profit to operate the preserved branch for the public joint powers authority that bought it. Volunteers began running trains in the autumn of 2010, and in spring 2011 repaired a washout that let passenger trains reach Latrobe for the first time in more than 50 years. Excursions have run as seasonal themed trips rather than to a regular headway. As of August 2026 the operator's own site says train operations are temporarily on hold for track repairs, with rides announced to resume later in 2026; the drawn years therefore stop at 2025 rather than assert service through the pause.
